clue.text: Wife desires charming women …

parts.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife, straight off the crossword's own list
to itch for something is to desire it, and the verb agrees in number

explanation.surface: A wife hankering after glamorous company, the thought running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' is not flattery here but a job description: these are women who work charms, and the ellipsis hands the sentence on to 5 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A witch charms in the sense of casting spells, so 'charming women' names the trade rather than paying a compliment.

clue.text: Add in what I did here, as stated

parts.note: the clue's own little word, taken at face value

indicators.note: Stated means spoken rather than written, so what follows is spelled the way it sounds instead of the way its source word looks.

parts.note: The setter is talking from inside his own puzzle: what he did here was write clues, and that word said aloud comes out with its letters in this order.

explanation.surface: The setter breaking off mid-sentence to remark on the job he has just done.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters refer to themselves and their own work inside clues all the time, and 'I' here is the man who wrote the puzzle you are holding.
explanation.definitionFit: To include something is to add it to a list or group, so 'Add' is the plain everyday verb for the same action.

clue.text: Summit's within Worcester, centrally, elevated

indicators.note: The letters wanted are not at either end of the phrase but in the middle of it, straddling the gap between two words.
Raised up, and in a down entry that means the buried letters are read from the bottom of the grid upwards.

parts.note: Five consecutive letters sit across the gap between these two words, running the wrong way.

explanation.surface: A high point somewhere in the middle of Worcester, as though the city had a peak of its own.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden runs that also need turning round are the hardest to see, and this one starts on the last letter of a word nobody rereads.
explanation.definitionFit: The crown of a hill or a road is its highest point, a topographical sense of the word a long way from the king's headgear.

clue.text: Use charm to control tendency to avoid pressure

indicators.note: Avoiding something means keeping clear of it, so the letter named next is the one the word has to do without.

parts.note: a penchant is a leaning or tendency towards something
P is the standing abbreviation for pressure, as in physics

explanation.surface: Advice on handling people: win them over rather than leaning on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To avoid pressure' reads as more of the same management advice and is really a deletion order — the trap is taking the whole second half for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To enchant someone is to charm them so completely that they do as you wish, which is the 'control' half of the definition.

clue.text: … valour is boring her — ordinary and primarily 'macho'

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so this word sits inside the others

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of macho is used

parts.note: the first letter of macho

explanation.surface: Following on from the witches, a woman finds plain macho bravery tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' is not tedious but drilling: IS bores into HER, O and M (the first letter of 'macho'), going between O and M.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroism is great bravery, and valour is a literary word for courage in battle.

clue.text: Barrier dropped to protect pupil

definitions.meaning: The other kind of pupil is the black circle at the centre of an eye, and what drops over it is a fold of skin.
The surface sends you to school, where a pupil is a child and a barrier coming down sounds like a safety gate.

explanation.surface: A safety gate coming down to keep a schoolchild out of harm's way.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves change meaning at once: the pupil is the one in your eye, and the barrier is the shutter of skin that falls over it whenever anything comes near.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelid is exactly a flap that drops to shield the pupil, so the clue is a straight description with one word quietly doing double duty.

clue.text: Toast peer performing in musical dramas

indicators.note: Performing is what a company does with a script — the same material delivered in a fresh arrangement each night.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters — exactly the enumeration

explanation.surface: A titled actor being toasted for his turn on the light-opera stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hands you a lord treading the boards, and both of its opening words are really only letters; 'in' is a joint here, not a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An operetta is a short, light opera with spoken dialogue — musical drama on a smaller scale — and both definition and answer are plural.

clue.text: Rise up, capturing aged warrior

indicators.note: capturing means holding prisoner, so the rearranged letters surround the next piece
up as in something being up, out of order, so the letters of rise are stirred

parts.note: aged means old

explanation.surface: A call for a rebellion that seizes an elderly fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise up' reads as a call to revolt, but 'up' stirs RISE into S and IER, which go around OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier is a member of an army, a fighting man or warrior.

clue.text: White dominance troubling viewers

definitions.meaning: The surface reads as politics, one race on top; the setter means a landscape with nothing in it but white.
Not an audience objecting to a broadcast — the trouble is in the eyes of anyone who looks at that landscape too long.

explanation.surface: A headline about racial supremacy and the offence it causes the people watching.
explanation.walkthrough: Glare off an unbroken snowfield burns the surface of the eye and takes a climber's sight away for a day or two — the condition mountaineers wear goggles against.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow blindness is temporary sight loss caused by too much white glare, so the clue names its cause and its effect in the same breath.

clue.text: E-copy

definitions.meaning: the letter as the radio alphabet says it, alongside Alpha, Bravo and Charlie
to copy someone is to give back what they just said

explanation.surface: An e-copy: the digital version of a document.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen does the whole of the misdirection, gluing two separate definitions into one modern-sounding compound that means neither of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio operators say Echo for the letter E, and an echo is a sound that copies what was said — two everyday senses sitting a hyphen apart.

clue.text: Tale of servitude recalled in reels

indicators.note: Something that reels is staggering, unsteady on its feet, so the letters in front of it cannot keep their footing either.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters — the enumeration matches exactly

explanation.surface: A story of drudgery being remembered while the film spools turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' looks like a reversal instruction and 'in' like a container one; both are only fodder, and the single instruction in the clue is its last word.
explanation.definitionFit: The girl of the fairy tale is kept as a household drudge by her stepmother, and the story carries her name, so it defines the tale itself.

clue.text: One in five heading to Open are seeds

definitions.note: The answer is a mass noun — one crop made of countless grains — so a plural definition is fair even though the word itself takes a singular verb.

parts.note: a quin is one of a set of quintuplets — one baby in five

indicators.note: A heading is what stands at the top of something, so only the front letter of each word after it is wanted.

parts.note: the first letters of these two words, in the order they stand

explanation.surface: Tennis talk: a fifth of the players arriving at the Open are the seeded ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seeds' is the tennis word the whole surface is built for, and the definition wants the kitchen kind — the grain sold as a health food.
explanation.definitionFit: Quinoa is grown and eaten for its seed heads, so 'seeds' says what the crop physically is rather than describing it loosely.

clue.text: Remain on the right side of suspicious cook — porky but harmless?

indicators.note: In an across entry the right-hand side is the later half, so the piece named first ends up second in the grid.

parts.note: Mrs White is the cook in Cluedo, the British murder-mystery board game, and one of its six suspects.
to lie somewhere is to remain there — the resting verb, nothing to do with untruth

explanation.surface: Staying in the good books of a cook who suspects you, with a fib told to keep the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porky' is rhyming slang — a pork pie is a lie — and the other half comes from a board game whose suspects are all named after colours.
explanation.definitionFit: A porky is a lie in rhyming slang, and the white sort is the harmless one told to spare someone's feelings rather than to deceive them.

clue.text: Way to find a giant, live, and chat about man's missing head?

parts.note: to be is to exist or live

indicators.note: missing head means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: the word man with its possessive s
to chat about something is to talk

explanation.surface: Advice on tracking down a giant: exist, and gossip about a beheaded man.
explanation.walkthrough: In the fairy tale Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack climbs the beanstalk to reach the giant's castle. 'Missing head' takes the M off MAN'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack climbs a magic beanstalk up to the land of the giant, so it is his route there.

clue.text: Dark approaching, tenses, one male, alone at the end

parts.note: nigh is the old word for near, as in 'the end is nigh'
T is grammar's abbreviation for tense, and the plural doubles it
the Roman numeral
M is what any form prints beside the box for male

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, and that single letter is all this instruction hands over.

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A horror-film logline: dark coming on, one man tense, and finally nobody left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alone at the end' reads as a fate and works as an instruction, which is where the last letter comes from. Everything before it is a stack of one- and two-letter conventions worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: Nighttime is the stretch of hours when it is dark, so 'Dark' used as a noun — the dark — stands in for it exactly.

clue.text: Censors essentially blue tale

indicators.note: The essence of a word is what sits at its very centre, so this asks for the middle letter alone.

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven, with three standing either side
Blue is the colour of the Conservative party in Britain, whose members are Tories.

explanation.surface: Censors reacting to a blue tale — a smutty piece getting cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' means smutty in the surface and party-political in the wordplay, and the last word of the sentence is the only one doing an honest job.
explanation.definitionFit: A story and a tale are the same object, a narrative told for entertainment — an everyday synonym with no crossword trickery in it.

clue.text: Barnaby ousts Romeo and takes Juliet — he's a trier!

indicators.note: ousts means drives out, so that letter is removed from the surname
takes means accepts another letter in its place

parts.note: Barnaby Rudge is the title character of a Dickens novel
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Juliet is J in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A romantic triangle: Barnaby elbows aside Romeo, wins Juliet and is praised for effort.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Juliet are not the lovers but NATO letters R and J; Barnaby is Dickens's Barnaby Rudge. 'A trier' is not one who keeps trying but one who tries cases.
explanation.definitionFit: A judge hears and decides cases in court, which is literally to try them.

clue.text: Odd you twice caught group of students drawn in by unframed Dali

indicators.note: To catch something is to hold it fast, so the letters either side close around whatever they have caught.
Drawn in means pulled inside, saying a second time that the middle piece sits within the outer ones.
A frame goes round the outside of a picture, so taking it off strips the first and last letters.

parts.note: the second of the pair, closing the trap behind them
the painter's name with its outer letters taken away
The NUS is Britain's National Union of Students, the body college student unions belong to.
the letter whose name is 'you', and this is the first of the two

explanation.surface: A Dali canvas out of its frame, with a crowd of students pulled towards it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' is the painter's word doing an insertion's job and 'unframed' is his word for a deletion, which is how the art-gallery surface hides two instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Unusual and odd both mean out of the ordinary, and either adjective slots into the same sentence without a change of grammar.

clue.text: INXS provided Yates's first shoot up

parts.note: The band's name read out letter by letter: its X is the Roman numeral ten, so it spells longer than it looks.
provided that = if, the conditional conjunction

indicators.note: The first of a name is its opening letter, and just that one letter joins the assembly.

parts.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A tabloid line about the band INXS, Yates, and a first injection.
explanation.walkthrough: X is ten in Roman numerals, which is what turns a four-letter band name into six letters of the answer. 'Shoot up' means to rise sharply, not what the surface implies.
explanation.definitionFit: Prices and numbers that shoot up rise steeply, and to intensify is to grow rapidly stronger — the same movement, as a verb.

clue.text: Overlooked, start off angry, swear endlessly inside

indicators.note: Starting a word off takes its start away — the opening letter is what goes.
Without an end, so the final letter comes off before the piece is used.
The letters named just before this word go within the piece already built, not after it.

parts.note: angry is VEXED, and starting it off loses the V
to swear is to cuss, and the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Being passed over, going red, and swearing endlessly under your breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooked' has two senses and the clue wants the forgiving one — a fault overlooked is a fault let off. Both deletions hide inside the tantrum the surface describes.
explanation.definitionFit: To excuse an offence is to overlook it, letting it pass without penalty, and the past participle matches the answer's -ed ending.

clue.text: Most rewarding transposing soprano flute line

indicators.note: Transposing is putting things into each other's places, which is what happens to the letters gathered after it.

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for soprano on a score
the word itself, five of the seven letters
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A soprano and a flute swapping parts in an orchestral score.
explanation.walkthrough: The music is all surface: a singer, an instrument and a line of the score are three chunks of letters, and transposing is the musician's word for moving them.
explanation.definitionFit: Living life to the fullest means getting the most out of it, so 'Most rewarding' matches both the sense and the superlative ending.

clue.text: This setter's regularly upset with contrary editor's delay

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I, and this setter's, with the 's read as is, gives I'M

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of upset

indicators.note: contrary means facing the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A setter is annoyed by a stubborn editor holding things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' is not an anagram signal but the word taken 'regularly' for PE; 'contrary' turns ED into DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To impede something is to hinder or obstruct it, which slows or delays its progress.

clue.text: Barbarian, turning good guy, with trimmed locks — he's chasing foxy type?

parts.note: the Huns were barbarian invaders of the Roman Empire

indicators.note: turning means the two letters are flipped round

parts.note: ST, short for saint, is a good person

indicators.note: trimmed means cut back, losing the final letter

parts.note: a mane is a long, thick head of hair

explanation.surface: A wild man transformed into a hero with a haircut goes after an alluring woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foxy type' hints at a seductive person but means a fox itself. 'Turning' flips ST to TS, and 'trimmed' cuts MANE to MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A huntsman rides with hounds in a fox hunt, so he pursues a fox.

clue.text: Move to try and cover King's naked glee after fling

definitions.text: Move to try and cover King

indicators.note: Stripped of its covering, so the word gives up its outer letters and keeps only what was underneath.

parts.note: to cast is to fling — the throwing verb, as in casting a line

indicators.note: Coming along behind, so the letters named before it take the later position.

parts.note: the inner two letters, with the outer ones taken off

explanation.surface: Gossip about a king's undisguised delight after an affair, and a move to cover it up.
explanation.walkthrough: Castling is the one chess move that shifts two pieces at once, tucking the king into a corner behind a rook, so 'cover King' describes it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess, to castle is to move king and rook together so that the king ends up shielded, which is what the definition spells out.

clue.text: Catch spots orally

indicators.note: By mouth — the word is handed over as a noise, so what you write in the grid is a different spelling of it.

parts.note: To spot something is to see it, and that verb said aloud is written this way in the grid.

explanation.surface: Catching a spotty illness by mouth, as though measles were something you swallow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' is the everyday verb for noticing rather than the marks on a face, and the pun about catching a disease is what makes the surface hold together.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize something is to catch hold of it suddenly, so 'Catch' is the plain verb for the same grabbing action.

clue.text: Ventures boundless flair inspired by coaches

indicators.note: Without bounds — the first and last letters, the ones that bound the word, are taken away.
To inspire is to breathe in, so this piece is drawn inside the one named next.

parts.note: a coach is a long-distance bus, and this word splits to make room
flair is finesse, arriving with its outer letters gone

explanation.surface: Sports coaches inspiring limitless flair in the players they train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coaches' are the vehicles rather than the trainers, and 'inspired' is being used in its old sense of breathing in — both words are pulling towards the sporting surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A business is a commercial venture, so the two plurals are everyday synonyms for the enterprises people set up and run.

clue.text: Once partner is following, beginning to introduce glimpse of billy goat

indicators.note: Following means coming along behind, so this piece takes the final position in the assembly.
A glimpse is the briefest sight of something — here, just the letter it starts with.
The beginning of a word is its opening letter, and no more than that is taken.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
the first letter of the word for a male goat
a partner one used to have is an ex

explanation.surface: An ex tagging along while someone starts to make the introductions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Billy goat' looks like a single phrase and the setter splits it down the middle: the first half is wordplay and the second is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ibex is a wild mountain goat with huge curved horns, so 'goat' defines it by its family — the general word standing for the particular animal.

clue.text: One holding up the line returning skins again?

indicators.note: To return is to come back the way you went, so in an across entry these letters are read from the right.

parts.note: to skin a potato is to peel it, and doing it a second time puts RE on the front

explanation.surface: Someone at the front of the queue holding everyone up, handing back peel a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: A sleeper is one of the timber beams laid under a railway track, so it holds the line up in the most literal way while the surface has you standing in a queue.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway sleepers are the crosswise beams that carry the rails, so 'one holding up the line' is a plain job description of the object.

clue.text: Trailers way back, after about 5½ days travelling west

indicators.note: Back means turned round, so the two letters of that piece land in the opposite order.
West is leftwards on a map and on the grid, so this run of letters is read from its far end.

parts.note: re = about, the word at the head of a memo
the Roman numeral for five
half of the word 'days', the first two of its four letters
a street is a way, and ST is how it is written on an envelope

explanation.surface: A convoy of caravans heading west after five and a half days on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trailers' are cinema previews in the definition and caravans in the surface, and halving a written word to take its first two letters is a device worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer is the short film a cinema runs to advertise a coming release, so the two plurals name the same thing in different trades.
